positions.moves: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e3 b5
positions.then: a4 c6 axb5 cxb5 Qf3
positions.why: The pawn on b5 is all that holds c4, and it cannot be held up itself. 4. a4 attacks it at once, and every answer loses something: 4... c6 5. axb5 cxb5 6. Qf3 wins a piece on the long diagonal; 4... a6 5. axb5, and the a-pawn is pinned to its rook (5... axb5 6. Rxa8); 4... bxa4 5. Qxa4+ and 4... b4 5. Bxc4 give the pawn back with Black's queenside wrecked. A quiet move such as 4. Nf3 gives Black time to shore the chain up with ...c6, and most of your advantage is gone. In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, undermine the b5 pawn before you develop.

positions.then: Qf3 Nc6 Qxc6+ Bd7 Qa6
positions.why: The c-pawn has left the long diagonal, and the rook on a8 stands at the end of it with nothing defended to put in between. 6. Qf3 attacks it, and Black must give up a piece to save it: 6... Nc6 7. Qxc6+ Bd7 8. Qa6, or 6... Bb7 7. Qxb7. This is the point of 4. a4: once the pawns on b5 and c6 have been traded off, the diagonal is open. When a pawn chain is taken apart, look at the lines its pawns were closing.

positions.then: Bxc4 Bb4+ Nbd2 Nc6 O-O Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nb3 Be7 Nbxd4
positions.why: Nothing has to be taken back on d4 yet. 5. Qxd4 Qxd4 6. Nxd4 trades the queens, and your lead in development with them; 5. Nxd4 lets Black develop with tempo by ...Bc5. 5. Bxc4 wins back the pawn that matters, brings a piece out and aims at f7: after 5... Nc6 6. O-O or 5... Bb4+ 6. Nbd2 Nc6 7. O-O you are ready for e5 and Nb3, and the d4 pawn falls in the end. Holding on to it is punished at once: 5... c5 6. Ne5 Be6 7. Bxe6 fxe6 8. Qh5+. When you are ahead in development, develop again before you recapture.

A centre pawn that is attacked and can advance with tempo usually should.

positions.source: opening theory; the author's game ea29c721 reached it by 2... dxc4 3. Nc3 Nc6 (he played 4. e3: no card)
positions.why: The knight on c6 has no good square to go to, so chase it: 4. d5. On a5 it is lost to 5. Qa4+ c6 6. b4; on e5 it is hit again by 5. f4, and e4 follows with a broad centre; going home to b8 costs Black two moves. You had this position in a game and played 4. e3: that wins the pawn back, but lets Black free the game with ...e5. When a piece stands in front of your pawn with nowhere good to go, push the pawn before you develop.

positions.then: Qb3 Qb6 Qxb6 axb6 cxd5 cxd5 Nxd5
positions.why: The bishop has left b7 without a defender, and d5 is under fire as well: 4. Qb3 hits both, and Black cannot hold both. 4... Qb6 5. Qxb6 axb6 6. cxd5 wins a pawn, since 6... cxd5 runs into 7. Nxd5, with a fork on c7 and the b6 pawn hanging; 4... dxc4 5. Qxb7; and 4... b6 or 4... Qc7 costs at least a pawn after 5. cxd5. This is why the Slav bishop waits for ...Nf6 and ...dxc4 before it comes out. Whenever the c8 bishop leaves home early in a d4 opening, look at Qb3 first.

positions.then: cxd5 Nxd5 Nf3 e6 e4 Nf6 Nc3
positions.source: opening theory; the author's game efb9bf83 from the other side (he played 2... Nf6 as Black, and met 3. Nc3)
positions.why: A knight does not hold d5 the way a pawn does. Take: 3. cxd5. After 3... Nxd5 the knight is a target for e4, best prepared by 4. Nf3 (4. e4 at once allows 4... Nf6 5. Nc3 e5); after 3... Qxd5 4. Nc3 the queen is chased with tempo. Either way you get the whole centre. The routine 3. Nc3 lets Black off: 3... e6 or 3... c6 is an ordinary Queen's Gambit Declined or Slav. When the pawn you attack is defended only by pieces, capture, and take the centre from the piece that recaptures.

It is the same answer as to 1... c5 on the first move: when a wing pawn attacks your d4 pawn and d5 is free, advance.

title: Queen's Gambit Declined, Black takes on c4

positions.moves: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 dxc4
positions.then: e4 Nf6 Bxc4 c5 Nf3
positions.why: Black has given up the centre and shut the c8 bishop in behind e6: the worst of the Queen's Gambit Accepted. Take all of the centre at once: 4. e4, and the bishop takes on c4 next move. The pawn cannot be kept: 4... b5 just loses it to 5. Nxb5. 4. e3 also wins the pawn back, but with half the centre. When they give you the centre for nothing, take both squares.

positions.why: The pawn on d4 is the point of Black's gambit, and the natural way to challenge it is the one that loses: 4. e3 Bb4+ 5. Bd2 dxe3, and now 6. Bxb4 exf2+ 7. Ke2 fxg1=N+ wins for Black (the Lasker Trap), while 6. fxe3 leaves you with broken pawns and nothing for them. Attack the pawn with a piece instead: 4. Nf3, and after 4... Nc6 go on developing around it with a3, g3 or Nbd2 (any of those is as good at once, and the card takes them). You are a pawn up, and it is Black who has something to prove. When an advanced pawn can answer e3 with a check and a capture, bring pieces to bear on it first.

title: Italian Four Knights, the fork trick

positions.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Nc3
positions.then: Nxe4 Nxe4 d5 Bd3 dxe4 Bxe4 Bd6
positions.source: the author's games (77283091, aef78837, 47fe0bf8, 3e4d5f6a, ebeb664c: he played ...Bc5 or ...Bb4, no card)
positions.why: The fork trick. 4... Nxe4 gives up the knight for a moment: after 5. Nxe4 d5 the pawn forks bishop and knight, you take one of them back, and you are left with the centre and easy development (6. Bd3 dxe4 7. Bxe4 Bd6). 5. Bxf7+ Kxf7 6. Nxe4 d5 is better still for you, and 5. O-O Nxc3 6. dxc3 f6 leaves you a pawn up. You have had this position five times, by 3. Bc4 or by 3. Nc3, and played ...Bc5 or ...Bb4 each time: sound, but this is the move that takes the centre. With a bishop on c4 and a knight on c3 against your knight on f6, look for ...Nxe4 and ...d5.

title: Italian Four Knights, the fork trick

positions.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Nc3 Nxe4 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Nxe4
positions.then: d5 Ng3 e4 Ng1
positions.why: White has given the bishop back for a pawn to pull your king out, and it does not work: you have the two bishops and the centre, if you take it now. 6... d5 hits the knight, and it has no good square: 7. Ng3 e4 sends the other knight home to g1, and 7. Neg5+ Kg8 leaves both knights to be driven back by ...h6 and ...e4. The king walks to safety on g8 by hand. Bxf7+ in the fork trick is nothing to fear: answer it with the centre.

positions.why: The knight on e4 is pinned to your king and attacked, and one move both holds it and hits back: 6... d5 defends it and attacks the bishop. After 7. Bxd5 Qxd5 8. Nc3 the knight on c3 cannot be taken (the d-pawn is pinned to your queen, the e4 knight to your king), so the queen steps aside, to a5 or h5, and after 9. Nxe4 Be6 the game is level. Anything slower loses material: 6... Be7 7. Rxe4 d5 8. Rxe7+, or 6... f5 7. Bg5. On an open e-file with your king still on e8, meet the pin with a move that makes a threat.

positions.why: You are a pawn down, and the way to make that not matter is to give it up for good: 6... c6 7. dxc6 bxc6, and the bishop must move again. After 8. Be2 h6 9. Nf3 e4 10. Ne5 Bd6 every move of yours has come with a threat, and your pieces are out while White's go backwards. 6... Bd7 is playable, but after 7. Qe2 White keeps the pawn in more comfort. In the Two Knights with 5... Na5 you are playing for time, not for the pawn: do not stop to count it.

positions.moves: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 f4
positions.then: d5 fxe5 Nxe4 Nf3 Be7
positions.why: This is not a King's Gambit: with your knight already on f6, 3... exf4 is a mistake, because 4. e5 sends it home (4... Ng8; 4... Qe7 5. Qe2 only makes it worse). Strike in the centre instead: 3... d5. After 4. fxe5 Nxe4 your knight has a fine square in the middle of the board; after 4. exd5 Nxd5 you are simply well developed. A wing gambit while your king's knight can be hit by e5: answer in the centre.

positions.then: Ng6 e5 Ng8 Bc4 d5 Bxd5 N8e7
positions.why: You are a piece up, and all White has for it is pawns that gain time on your knights. Put this one where they gain least: 5... Ng6 6. e5 Ng8 7. Bc4 d5, giving a pawn back to get the pieces out, and the extra knight tells. 5... Nc6 looks more natural and is much harder to play: 6. d5 hits it again, and after 6... Ne5 7. f4 Ng6 8. e5 both knights are being chased. A piece ahead against a pawn storm: retreat to where the pawns cannot follow with tempo, and give something back to develop.

positions.then: dxc6 Nxe5 Qd4 Nf3 Qxe4+ Qe2 Qxe2+ Kxe2
positions.why: Take towards the open lines: 4... dxc6 opens the d-file for the queen and a diagonal for the c8 bishop, and you have the two bishops to use on them. The pawn on e5 is not hanging: 5. Nxe5 Qd4 forks knight and e-pawn and wins it back at once (6. Nf3 Qxe4+). 4... bxc6 takes towards the centre, as the rule says, and here it is the lesser move: the bishops stay shut in, and White gets a free hand in the centre with 5. d4 or 5. Nc3. Capture towards the centre unless the other capture opens lines for pieces that need them.

title: Queen's Gambit Declined, the Elephant Trap

positions.moves: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Nbd7 cxd5 exd5 Nxd5
positions.then: Nxd5 Bxd8 Bb4+ Qd2 Bxd2+ Kxd2 Kxd8
positions.why: The knight on f6 looked pinned to the queen. It is not: 6... Nxd5 7. Bxd8 Bb4+, and the only way out of check is to put the queen in the way: 8. Qd2 Bxd2+ 9. Kxd2 Kxd8. When the dust settles you are a knight up for a pawn. A pin on the queen holds only while the pinned piece has no forcing move of its own: look for the check that wins the queen back.

positions.then: c4 Qc2 Bf5 Qc1 Nh5
positions.why: The queens face each other, and whoever takes opens the a-file for the other side: 6... Qxb3 7. axb3 gives White's rook a file and a small pull. Make White decide instead: 6... c4 hits the queen. After 7. Qxb6 axb6 it is your rook that has the open file, and ...b5 and ...b4 come fast; after 7. Qc2 Bf5 the bishop arrives with tempo, because 8. Qxf5 Qxb2 wins the rook in the corner. When queens stand off on the b-file, push the pawn that makes the other side take.
